title: Metoprolol and Alcohol: Is It Safe to Drink on a Beta Blocker?
excerpt: Can you drink on metoprolol? How alcohol and metoprolol add up to lower blood pressure, tartrate vs. succinate, why you should never skip a dose, and warning signs.
metaDescription: Can you drink on metoprolol? How alcohol and metoprolol lower blood pressure together, tartrate vs. succinate, why never to skip a dose, and warning signs.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** most people who take metoprolol can have an occasional drink, and many doctors are fine with one drink with a meal. The problem is that alcohol and metoprolol push in the same direction. Both can lower your blood pressure, and metoprolol also stops your heart from speeding up to make up for it. Put them together and some people get dizzy, light-headed, or faint, especially when they stand up quickly, drink more than usual, or drink on an empty stomach. Regular heavy drinking causes a different problem: it raises blood pressure and can trigger heart rhythm trouble, which works against the very reason you were prescribed metoprolol.

**The quick rules:** Never skip, delay, or stop a metoprolol dose so you can drink. Stopping suddenly can cause a dangerous rebound in heart rate and blood pressure, and the label carries a boxed warning about it. Keep drinks light and slow, eat first, drink water alongside, and stand up slowly. Be extra careful the first few times you drink after starting metoprolol or changing the dose. If you take the tartrate form (Lopressor), take it with food as directed. If you have diabetes, know that metoprolol can hide some warning signs of low blood sugar, and alcohol makes low blood sugar more likely.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains how metoprolol and alcohol interact in general terms. It is not a substitute for advice from the doctor or pharmacist who knows your heart condition, your dose, and your other medicines. **Talk to your doctor before drinking on metoprolol if** you take it for heart failure, after a heart attack, for angina, or for atrial fibrillation, if you also take a water pill or other blood pressure medicine, or if you have diabetes. **Get medical help right away (call 911 in the US) if** you faint, have chest pain, struggle to breathe, have a very slow pulse with dizziness or confusion, or feel your heart racing or fluttering in a way that doesn't settle.

## How Metoprolol and Alcohol Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

Metoprolol is a **beta blocker**. It blocks the effect of adrenaline on beta-1 receptors, which sit mostly in the heart. That makes your heart beat more slowly and less forcefully, which lowers blood pressure, eases the heart's workload, and steadies some fast heart rhythms. Doctors call it "cardioselective" because it mainly targets the heart rather than the lungs and blood vessels, unlike older beta blockers such as propranolol.

Alcohol affects the same system from a different angle. In the hours after a drink or two, alcohol widens blood vessels (vasodilation), which tends to lower blood pressure for a while. That's the warm, flushed feeling. Normally your body notices the drop and responds by speeding up your heart a little to keep blood flowing to your brain. That reflex is exactly what metoprolol dampens.

So the interaction is not a chemical clash in the liver. It's an **additive effect on your circulation**:

1. **Alcohol lowers blood pressure in the short term** by relaxing blood vessels.
2. **Metoprolol lowers blood pressure** and slows the heart.
3. **Your safety reflex is blunted.** With metoprolol on board, your heart can't speed up as much to compensate when your blood pressure dips.

The result for most people at low amounts is nothing noticeable. For some, it's a wave of dizziness when they stand up, a feeling of being more tipsy than expected, or in the worst case a faint. Doctors call the stand-up version **orthostatic hypotension**, which just means a drop in blood pressure when you change position.

### Does alcohol change metoprolol levels in your blood?

Not in any way that matters for most people. Metoprolol is broken down mainly by a liver enzyme called **CYP2D6**. Alcohol is handled mostly by different enzymes, so a normal amount of drinking isn't known to raise or lower your metoprolol levels in a meaningful way. The interaction is about what the two do to your blood vessels and heart, not about one drug changing the other's dose.

There is one indirect wrinkle worth knowing. Some over-the-counter products people reach for on a drinking night, especially the sleep-aid antihistamine **diphenhydramine** (Benadryl, the "PM" in many night-time pain relievers), can slow CYP2D6 and raise metoprolol levels. More on that in the hangover section below.

### The long-term story is the opposite of the short-term one

Here's the part that confuses people. A drink or two lowers blood pressure for a few hours. But **regular heavy drinking raises blood pressure** over weeks and months, and it's one of the more common reversible causes of high blood pressure. Blood pressure can also bounce higher the morning after a heavy night. So if you take metoprolol for hypertension and drink heavily most days, the alcohol is quietly working against your medicine. Our guide to [alcohol and blood pressure](/never-hungover/alcohol-hypertension-blood-pressure-management-2025) explains that rebound effect in more detail.

## Metoprolol Tartrate vs. Metoprolol Succinate: Does the Form Matter?

Metoprolol comes in two main forms, and they're not interchangeable milligram for milligram. Check your bottle so you know which one you take.

| | Metoprolol tartrate | Metoprolol succinate |
|---|---|---|
| Common brand | Lopressor | Toprol-XL |
| Release | Immediate release | Extended release (ER/XL) |
| Usual dosing | Usually twice a day | Usually once a day |
| Food | Label says take with or right after a meal | Can be taken with or without food, but be consistent |
| Common uses | High blood pressure, angina, after a heart attack | High blood pressure, angina, heart failure |
| Alcohol angle | Blood levels peak a few hours after each dose, so drinking near a dose can stack the effects more sharply | Steadier levels through the day, so timing matters a bit less, but the additive effect is still there |

**For tartrate users:** because the tablet releases quickly, blood levels peak within a few hours of a dose. If you take your evening dose right before going out, the peak of the drug and the peak of the alcohol can line up. That doesn't mean you should move or skip the dose. It means the evening after a dose is when you should be most careful about how much you drink and how quickly you stand up. Taking tartrate with food, as the label directs, also smooths its absorption.

**For succinate users:** the extended-release tablet is built to release the drug slowly over the day. Swallow it whole or, if your tablet is scored, split it along the score line as your pharmacist directs. Don't crush or chew it, because that defeats the slow-release design. There's no special alcohol rule for metoprolol succinate on its label that changes how you take it, but the general caution about combined blood-pressure effects still applies.

**Combination pills:** some people take metoprolol combined with a water pill (hydrochlorothiazide), sold as Lopressor HCT or Dutoprol. A diuretic makes you lose fluid, and alcohol does too. That combination makes dehydration and dizziness on standing more likely, so drink extra water and be more conservative with alcohol.

## Why You Should Never Skip a Dose to Drink

This is the single most important point on this page. Some people think they're being careful by skipping their metoprolol on a night they plan to drink. **That is more dangerous than the drink itself.**

Your body adapts to a beta blocker by making more beta receptors, or making them more sensitive. If you suddenly stop, adrenaline hits all those receptors at once. Heart rate and blood pressure can surge. For someone with coronary artery disease, that rebound can bring on worse chest pain (angina), a heart attack, or a dangerous heart rhythm. That's why the metoprolol label carries a **boxed warning**, the FDA's strongest kind, telling people not to stop it abruptly and telling doctors to taper it over one to two weeks if it needs to be stopped.

One missed dose isn't usually a crisis for most people, but deliberately skipping doses around drinking turns an occasional mistake into a habit. The safer rule is simple:

- **Take your dose at the usual time,** drinking night or not.
- **Adjust the alcohol, not the medicine.** If you're worried about the combination, have less to drink or skip the drink.
- **If you forget a dose,** take it when you remember unless it's nearly time for the next one. Don't double up. If you're unsure, ask your pharmacist.
- **If you want to stop metoprolol,** talk to your doctor about tapering. Don't stop on your own.

## How Much Can You Drink on Metoprolol?

There is no official safe number that applies to everyone on metoprolol. Your doctor's advice depends on why you take it, your dose, and your other conditions. What general heart and blood pressure guidance tends to say:

- **If you drink, keep it moderate.** The US Dietary Guidelines define moderate drinking as up to one drink a day for women and up to two for men, and they note that drinking less is better for health than drinking more. Many cardiologists suggest staying at or below that, and often lower for people with heart disease.
- **A "drink" is smaller than people think.** One standard drink is about 12 oz of regular beer, 5 oz of wine, or 1.5 oz of spirits. A large pour of wine or a craft IPA can easily be two. Our [alcohol content by drink](/never-hungover/alcohol-content-by-drink) guide breaks this down.
- **Binge drinking is the real hazard.** Four or five drinks in one sitting causes the biggest blood pressure swings, the most dehydration, and the most heart rhythm problems.

Some people are usually told to avoid alcohol or keep it very limited. Talk to your doctor before drinking if any of these apply:

| Reason you take metoprolol | Why alcohol needs extra care |
|---|---|
| **Heart failure** | Alcohol weakens heart muscle over time (alcoholic cardiomyopathy) and adds fluid and salt load. Many heart failure patients are advised to limit or avoid it. |
| **Atrial fibrillation** | Alcohol is a well-known AFib trigger, including after a single heavy night. |
| **After a heart attack or for angina** | Big blood pressure swings and the morning-after rebound add strain on a heart with narrowed arteries. |
| **High blood pressure** | Light drinking is often fine; regular heavy drinking pushes blood pressure up and can make the medicine look like it isn't working. |
| **Migraine prevention** | Some people find alcohol, especially red wine, triggers their migraines, which works against the reason for the prescription. |

## Alcohol, Metoprolol, and Atrial Fibrillation

Metoprolol is one of the most common drugs used to control heart rate in atrial fibrillation (AFib), a fast, irregular heartbeat. If that's why you take it, alcohol deserves a closer look.

Doctors have long noticed AFib episodes after heavy drinking, often over holidays or weekends. The nickname for it is **"holiday heart."** Alcohol can irritate the heart's electrical system, shift your body's salts (electrolytes), and raise adrenaline during withdrawal from a heavy night, all of which can tip a susceptible heart into AFib.

The strongest evidence comes from a randomized trial published in the *New England Journal of Medicine* in 2020. Researchers in Australia asked regular drinkers with AFib to either stop drinking or carry on as usual. The group that cut out alcohol had fewer AFib recurrences and spent less time in AFib over six months. That's a meaningful result because it tested the question directly rather than just observing drinkers.

What this means in practice: metoprolol slows your heart rate during AFib, but it doesn't make alcohol harmless for your rhythm. If you notice palpitations, a fluttering or pounding heartbeat, or an irregular pulse after drinking, tell your doctor. If it comes with chest pain, fainting, or shortness of breath, get help right away. Our article on a [racing heart after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) covers what's common and what isn't.

## Common Side Effects That Alcohol Can Make Worse

Metoprolol has its own side effects, and several overlap with what alcohol does. When they stack, people often blame the drink or the pill when it's really both.

- **Dizziness and light-headedness.** The most common combined effect. Worse when standing, in heat, after exercise, or when dehydrated.
- **Tiredness.** Metoprolol commonly causes fatigue, especially in the first weeks. Alcohol is a sedative. Together they can make you sleepier and slower than you expect, so don't drive after drinking on metoprolol, even if you feel only slightly affected.
- **Slow heart rate.** Metoprolol lowers your resting pulse by design. A pulse in the 50s can be normal on it, but a slow pulse with dizziness, confusion, or fainting is not.
- **Sleep disruption and vivid dreams.** Metoprolol can cause vivid dreams, nightmares, or trouble sleeping in some people. Alcohol also fragments sleep in the second half of the night. If your sleep is worse on drinking nights, both may be contributing.
- **Low mood.** Some people notice a flat or low mood on beta blockers, and alcohol is a depressant. If your mood dips, mention it to your doctor rather than drinking to cope.
- **Cold hands and feet.** A known beta blocker effect. Alcohol makes you feel warm but actually lets heat escape through the skin, so in cold weather the combination can leave you colder than you realize.

## Metoprolol, Alcohol, and Low Blood Sugar

If you have diabetes, especially if you use insulin or a sulfonylurea such as glipizide or glyburide, this section is important.

**Alcohol can cause low blood sugar.** While your liver is busy processing alcohol, it releases less glucose into your blood. The effect can show up hours later, including overnight, and is more likely if you drank without eating.

**Metoprolol can hide the warning signs.** Many of the early alarms for low blood sugar, like a pounding heart and shakiness, come from adrenaline. A beta blocker blunts those signals. Sweating usually still happens, so it becomes one of the more reliable clues. Hunger, confusion, irritability, and blurred vision can also still show up.

Together, that means a low can arrive later than expected and with fewer warning signs. If you have diabetes and take metoprolol:

- Eat when you drink, and have a snack before bed.
- Check your blood sugar before bed and, if your doctor recommends it, during the night or first thing in the morning.
- Make sure the people you're with know that confusion or odd behavior might be low blood sugar, not just drunkenness.
- Ask your doctor or diabetes educator for a personal plan.

## Hangovers on Metoprolol: What to Take and What to Avoid

A hangover on metoprolol can feel a little different. You may feel more washed out and light-headed than usual, because dehydration lowers your blood pressure and metoprolol keeps your heart from speeding up to compensate. Some people notice they're dizzy every time they stand up the morning after.

Helpful steps:

- **Rehydrate steadily.** Water, plus something with electrolytes if you've been sick or sweaty. Dehydration is a big part of why you feel faint.
- **Stand up in stages.** Sit on the edge of the bed for a minute before getting up.
- **Eat something.** It helps both blood sugar and nausea.
- **Take your morning dose as usual.** Don't skip it because you feel rough.
- **If you vomited soon after your dose,** don't automatically take another one. Call your pharmacist and ask what to do for your specific form and dose.

Be careful with common morning-after remedies:

| Remedy | What to know if you take metoprolol |
|---|---|
| **Acetaminophen (Tylenol)** | Doesn't interact with metoprolol. Stick to label doses and follow the alcohol warnings. See our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol). |
| **Ibuprofen, naproxen (NSAIDs)** | Regular use can raise blood pressure and weaken the effect of blood pressure medicines. They also carry a stomach bleeding warning for people who drink. An occasional single dose is less of a concern, but ask your doctor if you have heart failure or kidney problems. |
| **Decongestants (pseudoephedrine, phenylephrine)** | Can raise blood pressure and heart rate. Ask a pharmacist before using them with a blood pressure medicine. |
| **Diphenhydramine (Benadryl, many "PM" products)** | Can raise metoprolol levels by slowing the enzyme that breaks it down, and adds drowsiness on top of alcohol. Avoid it on drinking nights. |
| **Caffeine** | A normal cup of coffee is generally fine. Large amounts of energy drinks can raise heart rate and blood pressure and are best avoided, especially if you have AFib. |

### Don't take extra metoprolol for a racing heart

Some people notice their heart pounding the morning after drinking and are tempted to take an extra metoprolol to calm it. Don't. Extra doses can drop your heart rate and blood pressure too far, especially when you're dehydrated. If your heart is racing, irregular, or won't settle, call your doctor or get checked. If it comes with chest pain, fainting, or breathlessness, call 911.

## Metoprolol vs. Other Beta Blockers With Alcohol

The basic advice is the same across beta blockers: an occasional light drink is often fine, heavy drinking is not, and never stop the medicine to drink. The details differ a little.

- **Propranolol** is not cardioselective and enters the brain more easily. It's often used for anxiety and migraine, and it carries the same rebound warning. See our [propranolol and alcohol](/never-hungover/propranolol-and-alcohol) guide.
- **Carvedilol** also widens blood vessels, so dizziness on standing can be more pronounced. Its extended-release capsule (Coreg CR) has a specific label instruction about alcohol timing.
- **Atenolol** is cardioselective like metoprolol and is cleared mainly by the kidneys rather than the liver.

For the full comparison, see our [beta blockers and alcohol](/never-hungover/beta-blockers-and-alcohol) hub.

## When to See a Doctor

Talk to your doctor at your next visit, or sooner, if:

- You feel dizzy or light-headed most times you drink, even a small amount.
- You're having more than a couple of drinks most days and your blood pressure readings are creeping up.
- You notice palpitations, a fluttering heartbeat, or an irregular pulse after drinking.
- You have diabetes and have had a low blood sugar episode after drinking.
- You want to cut back on drinking or stop metoprolol. Both are worth planning with your doctor.

**Get emergency help (call 911 in the US) if you or someone with you:**

- Faints or nearly faints and doesn't recover quickly
- Has chest pain, pressure, or tightness
- Is short of breath or wheezing
- Has a very slow pulse along with confusion, extreme weakness, or fainting
- Has a fast, irregular heartbeat with dizziness or chest discomfort
- Shows signs of alcohol poisoning, such as vomiting while confused, very slow or irregular breathing, or being hard to wake

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

If you take metoprolol and you're searching for ways to feel better after drinking, the most reliable steps are the simple ones: drink less, drink slowly, eat first, and match each drink with water. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

Some people also use **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research is in animals and lab studies, with only limited human data. To be clear about what it can't do: there is no good evidence that DHM changes how metoprolol and alcohol interact, and it does not make heavier drinking safe for your heart or blood pressure. There are also no studies of DHM taken alongside metoprolol, so **ask your doctor or pharmacist before adding it**, as you would with any supplement while on heart medicine. Our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) explains what is and isn't known.

If your doctor says it's fine and you want to try it, two widely used options are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when.

## The Bottom Line

- Metoprolol and alcohol both lower blood pressure, and metoprolol blunts the heart's ability to compensate. The main risk is dizziness and fainting.
- An occasional light drink with food is often fine for people on metoprolol, but check with your doctor, especially if you have heart failure, AFib, angina, or diabetes.
- **Never skip or stop metoprolol to drink.** Stopping suddenly can cause a dangerous rebound.
- Regular heavy drinking raises blood pressure and triggers AFib, working against your medicine.
- On a hangover morning, rehydrate, stand up slowly, take your usual dose, avoid diphenhydramine and decongestants, and never take extra metoprolol for a racing heart.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can I drink alcohol while taking metoprolol?**

Many people can have an occasional drink, and many doctors allow light drinking on metoprolol. Both alcohol and metoprolol lower blood pressure, and metoprolol stops your heart from speeding up to compensate, so the main risk is dizziness or fainting. Keep it to one or two drinks with food, stand up slowly, and ask your doctor what's safe for your condition, especially if you take metoprolol for heart failure, AFib, or after a heart attack.

**Should I skip my metoprolol dose if I'm going to drink?**

No. Skipping or stopping metoprolol can cause a rebound rise in heart rate and blood pressure, and the label carries a boxed warning against stopping it suddenly because of the risk of worse chest pain, heart attack, or dangerous rhythms in people with heart disease. Take your dose as usual and adjust the alcohol instead.

**How long after taking metoprolol can I drink?**

There's no official waiting period. Metoprolol tartrate (Lopressor) peaks a few hours after each dose, so the evening after a dose is when the combined effect may be strongest. Metoprolol succinate (Toprol-XL) releases slowly over the day, so levels are steadier. Either way, the answer is not to move or skip doses, but to keep drinking light, eat first, and watch for dizziness.

**Is it different for metoprolol succinate and metoprolol tartrate?**

The interaction is the same: both forms add to alcohol's blood-pressure-lowering effect. Tartrate is immediate release and usually taken twice a day with food, so its peaks are sharper. Succinate is extended release and taken once a day, so levels are steadier. Don't crush or chew succinate tablets, and don't swap one form for the other without your doctor's direction.

**Can alcohol cause a slow heart rate on metoprolol?**

Alcohol usually raises heart rate a little, but on metoprolol your heart can't speed up as much, and heavy drinking, dehydration, or vomiting can leave you feeling faint. A pulse in the 50s can be normal on metoprolol. A slow pulse with dizziness, confusion, fainting, or shortness of breath is not, and needs prompt medical attention.

**Can I take metoprolol if I have a hangover?**

Yes, take your usual dose. Drink water, eat something, and stand up slowly, because dehydration plus metoprolol can make you light-headed. Avoid diphenhydramine (Benadryl and many PM products) and decongestants, and don't take extra metoprolol for a pounding heart. If your heartbeat is irregular or won't settle, call your doctor.

**Does alcohol make metoprolol less effective?**

An occasional drink doesn't stop metoprolol from working. Regular heavy drinking, though, raises blood pressure over time and can trigger atrial fibrillation, so it works against the reasons metoprolol is prescribed. If your readings are creeping up and you drink most days, the alcohol may be part of the reason.

**Is DHM safe to take with metoprolol?**

There are no studies of DHM taken with metoprolol, and there is no good evidence that DHM changes how metoprolol and alcohol interact or makes drinking safer for your heart. Ask your doctor or pharmacist before adding DHM or any supplement while you're on heart medication.
